scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that achievements have value, then argues they do not ensure a good life for the majority; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: A nation's famous artists and scientists can make its whole people proud.
One claim holds that the surest indicator of a great nation is the achievements of its rulers, artists, or scientists, on the reason that such achievements ensure a good life for most of its people.
I agree that achievements matter, but I disagree that they are the surest indicator or that they ensure a good life for the majority.
First, the achievements of a nation do carry real importance.
Great discoveries and works of art can improve lives and inspire a whole people.
For example, medical research and new technology have lengthened and eased countless ordinary lives.
This shows that achievements can sometimes raise the welfare of many people.
Such accomplishments can also give a nation pride and a strong sense of identity.
A country known for learning and creativity often earns respect around the world.
To this extent, the claim is not entirely wrong to value achievement.
Second, however, great achievements do not actually ensure a good life for most people.
A nation can produce brilliant art and science while the majority of its people stay poor.
Consider a country with world-famous scientists whose ordinary citizens still lack food and decent work.
Such cases show that achievement at the top does not automatically reach those at the bottom.
The welfare of all the people, not a few great works, is the truer test of national greatness.
Achievements built while the people suffer reveal a divided nation, not a great one.
The reason behind the claim, then, simply does not hold.
In conclusion, a nation's achievements are genuinely valuable and can improve many lives.
But they do not guarantee a good life for the majority, nor are they the surest sign of greatness.
The truest measure of a great nation is the welfare of all its people, not its achievements alone.
